title: Riemannian Flow Models with Reinforcement Learning for Molecular Crystal Structure Prediction
authors: Thomas Egg, Harry Winston Sullivan, Maya M. Martirossyan, Philipp Höllmer, Cheng Zeng, Adrian Roitberg
abstract: Crystal structure governs material properties, making crystal structure prediction (CSP) a fundamental problem in materials science. Generative models are a promising approach for solving this problem, but the prevalence of polymorphism, coupled with large unit cells and complex packing geometry, makes the molecular CSP task challenging for existing models. To address this, we introduce Coarse-Grained Open Materials Generation (CG-OMatG), an equivariant Riemannian flow-based generative model. CG-OMatG predicts molecular crystal structures \textit{via} a coarse-grained, hierarchical representation. CG-OMatG treats molecules as rigid bodies---performing both inter- and intra-molecular message passing to construct a geometric representation for molecular packings---and learns to reconstruct molecule centroid positions, orientations, and lattice parameters, conditioned on chemical species and conformer geometry. We train the model on subsets of the Open Molecular Crystals (OMC25) and Cambridge Structural Database (CSD) datasets. Further, we fine-tune the model \textit{via} policy gradient reinforcement learning to steer the model towards generating low-energy candidate structures. We validate the generated structures on the CSP blind test benchmark, assessing agreement with experimentally determined crystals using COMPACK packing-similarity analysis. CG-OMatG exhibits strong performance for generative molecular crystal structure prediction, paving the way for accelerated polymorph screening and organic solid-state materials discovery.

infographic.key_insight: CG-OMatG uses an equivariant, coarse-grained Riemannian flow model with reinforcement learning to generate molecular crystal structures by jointly predicting molecular positions, orientations, and lattice parameters.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This provides a practical path to faster polymorph screening and organic materials discovery by narrowing the search for low-energy crystal packings.
method: Rigid-body molecular representation with hierarchical inter- and intra-molecular message passing
Riemannian flow-based generation of centroid positions, orientations, and lattice parameters
Policy-gradient reinforcement learning to bias samples toward low-energy candidates
infographic.evidence_signal: The model is trained on subsets of OMC25 and CSD and evaluated on the CSP blind test benchmark using COMPACK packing-similarity comparisons to experimental crystals.
infographic.watch_item: Performance may depend on the quality and coverage of training data, and coarse-graining rigid molecules may be less suitable for highly flexible systems or unusual polymorphs.
infographic.paper_title: Riemannian Flow Models with Reinforcement Learning for Molecular Crystal Structure Prediction

title: From Automated Simulation to Autonomous Discovery: A Hierarchical Framework for Agentic Computational Materials Science
authors: Linggang Zhu, Jian Zhou, Zhimei Sun
abstract: The convergence of large language models, materials-specific foundation models, and agentic artificial intelligence is reshaping the paradigm of computational materials discovery. While high-throughput computation, automated workflows, and data-driven modeling have greatly expanded the scale of materials exploration, the core scientific decision-making loop remains largely human-directed. Agentic AI introduces the possibility of systems that can autonomously reason about materials objectives, execute simulations, and refine strategies. However, the rapid emergence of such systems has created a critical need for a unified and operational framework to define, evaluate, and guide scientific autonomy in computational materials discovery. In this Perspective, we propose the Computational Materials Agent Autonomy Level (CMA-AL) framework, a hierarchical taxonomy defining six levels of autonomous agency in computational materials science: scripted excecutor, LLM-assisted operator, adaptive explorer, experiment-ready modeler, agentic digital twin, and self-extending intelligence. We further map emerging agentic systems onto the framework and identify key scientific and technological challenges toward higher autonomy. CMA-AL provides a common language for characterizing agentic computational materials discovery, evaluating the maturity of emerging systems, and guiding their evolution toward increasingly autonomous materials discovery.

infographic.key_insight: The paper proposes CMA-AL, a six-level autonomy framework that defines how computational materials systems can progress from scripted simulation execution to self-extending discovery agents.
infographic.engineering_relevance: It gives researchers and platform builders a shared benchmark for designing, comparing, and scaling agentic AI workflows in materials simulation and discovery.
method: Defines six autonomy levels: scripted executor, LLM-assisted operator, adaptive explorer, experiment-ready modeler, agentic digital twin, and self-extending intelligence.
Maps emerging agentic materials systems onto the taxonomy to assess current maturity and gaps.
Identifies technical and scientific challenges needed to move toward higher autonomy.
infographic.evidence_signal: This is a perspective paper that synthesizes the field and proposes a conceptual framework; the abstract does not report new experimental data or benchmark results.
infographic.watch_item: The framework is conceptual, so practical adoption will depend on clear operational criteria and reliable evaluation metrics for autonomy across diverse materials workflows.
infographic.paper_title: From Automated Simulation to Autonomous Discovery: A Hierarchical Framework for Agentic Computational Materials Science

title: Co-PiLOT: Constrained Physics-Informed Latent Optimization for Target-Driven Inverse Design
authors: Mahish K. Guru, Mayank Nagar, Ayush vyas, Jan Bohlen, Roland Aydin, Noomane Ben Khalifa
abstract: Inverse design of physical systems (molecules, devices, microstructures) often reduces to optimizing a high-dimensional structure against an expensive black-box simulator. Direct search is difficult because the space is non-Euclidean, feasibility is hard to encode, and each evaluation is expensive. We present Co-PiLOT, a latent optimization approach that maps candidates through a generative encoder-decoder, uses the decoder as a learned validity prior, and searches the latent space with physics-informed black-box optimization. The framework is applied on the inverse design of magnesium alloy microstructure/texture. We develop a vision transformer based-encoder; paired with latent diffusion, diffusion transformer and rectified-flow transformer-based decoders on $\sim80{,}000$ EBSD-derived microstructure dataset to learn a minimal bottleneck, $z$. The ViT-FMDiT model ($z$=$768$) reconstructs high-fidelity microstructure images (FID $27.86$, MS-SSIM $0.178$), which our self-segmenting orientation codec converts into input grids for crystal plasticity solver. Finally, we introduce MERIDIAN, an active latent optimizer driven by deep-kernel Gaussian-process uncertainty, failure-aware feasibility prediction, manifold-aware trust regions, and target-aware acquisition. Within a budget of $160$ simulations, the ViT-FMDiT and MERIDIAN combination yields the best target-driven objective score, reducing the relative target error by $3$--$22\%$ against seven baselines (DANTE, TuRBO, BAxUS, CMA-ES, DDOM, SEIKO, DDPO) on the same decoder.

infographic.key_insight: Co-PiLOT turns inverse materials design into latent-space optimization by using a generative decoder as a validity prior and physics-informed search to find microstructures that better match target properties.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This enables more practical design of magnesium alloy microstructures by reducing dependence on costly simulator evaluations and improving feasibility in a hard-to-encode design space.
method: Encode EBSD-derived microstructure/texture images into a compact latent space with a Vision Transformer.
Decode candidates with latent diffusion / diffusion transformer / rectified-flow transformer models to enforce validity.
Optimize the latent variables with MERIDIAN, combining deep-kernel GP uncertainty, failure-aware feasibility prediction, manifold-aware trust regions, and target-aware acquisition.
infographic.evidence_signal: On about 80,000 EBSD-derived samples, the ViT-FMDiT decoder achieved strong reconstruction quality (FID 27.86, MS-SSIM 0.178), and with MERIDIAN under a 160-simulation budget it reduced relative target error by 3–22% versus seven baselines.
infographic.watch_item: Performance depends on the learned decoder and simulator fidelity, so generalization to new material systems or different solver settings may require retraining and careful validation.
infographic.paper_title: Co-PiLOT: Constrained Physics-Informed Latent Optimization for Target-Driven Inverse Design

title: Atoms to Processes: The Role of Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning in Chemical Engineering
authors: Michael Baldea, Linda J. Broadbelt, Marianthi G. Ierapetritou, Akhilesh Jain, Ankur Kumar, Thomas A. Kwan
abstract: The rapid maturation of artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) has catalyzed a profound shift in how chemical engineering problems are formulated, analyzed, and solved. Advances in computing, data availability, and learning algorithms have enabled AI/ML methods to impact applications spanning atomic-scale simulations, materials and catalyst discovery, transport and thermodynamics, separations, process systems engineering, and industrial operations. This article provides a perspective on recent methodological developments and representative applications, emphasizing how AI/ML tools are being integrated with first-principles models to address challenges of predictive accuracy, data scarcity, extrapolation, interpretability, and model lifecycle management. Across domains, a unifying trend is the move away from purely black-box approaches toward hybrid and physics-informed frameworks that explicitly respect conservation laws, thermodynamic consistency, and known structural constraints. These approaches not only improve robustness and reliability, but also enable meaningful human-AI collaboration by providing information at an appropriate level of abstraction for the task and decision context. We conclude that AI and ML are not replacing the core principles of chemical engineering; rather, they are amplifying them. As the field advances toward increasingly autonomous, adaptive, and sustainable systems, the thoughtful integration of AI/ML with first-principles understanding and domain expertise will be essential to realizing their full potential across both research and industrial practice.

infographic.key_insight: AI and machine learning are becoming core enablers in chemical engineering by combining data-driven prediction with first-principles knowledge across scales from atoms to full processes.
infographic.engineering_relevance: These methods can improve materials discovery, transport and thermodynamics modeling, separations, process design, and industrial operations while supporting more reliable and sustainable decision-making.
method: Hybrid physics-informed models that embed conservation laws and thermodynamic constraints
Machine learning integrated with first-principles simulations for prediction and discovery
Human-AI workflows that present information at the right abstraction level for engineering decisions
infographic.evidence_signal: The paper is a perspective synthesized from recent methodological developments and representative applications rather than a single benchmark study, emphasizing broad cross-domain adoption.
infographic.watch_item: A key implementation concern is managing data scarcity, extrapolation risk, interpretability, and model lifecycle maintenance when deploying AI/ML in high-stakes engineering settings.
infographic.paper_title: Atoms to Processes: The Role of Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning in Chemical Engineering

title: Long-Range Machine Learning Interatomic Potentials for Defect Energetics in SrTiO$_3$
authors: Yee Chit Wong, Marcel F. Langer, Reinhard J. Maurer, Nicholas D. M. Hine
abstract: Machine learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) have advanced rapidly in recent years, yet the majority of models remain semilocal in nature and neglect long-range electrostatic interactions. A growing number of long-range models have emerged to address this limitation, but systematic benchmarks comparing their performance on physically realistic systems remain scarce. In this work, we assess three long-range MLIPs -- MACE-POLAR, MACE-LES, and LOREM, against a short-range baseline MACE model, on their ability to capture long-range Coulombic interactions, progressing from idealised synthetic point-charge systems to first-principles data on realistic crystal structures. This progression allows us to isolate model's capability to learn electrostatic interactions from the many competing energy contributions, such as dielectric screening and exchange-correlation, that are present in DFT total energies. As a physically motivated benchmark system, we focus on strontium titanate SrTiO$_3$ with Sr--O Schottky vacancy pairs, a material in which long-range charge interactions play a central role and which serves as a natural stepping stone towards the study of charged polarons and other electronic and optical properties. Building on this benchmark, we further examine oxygen vacancy migration in the presence of the Sr--O Schottky pair, using climbing-image nudged elastic band calculations and molecular dynamics to obtain activation barriers as a function of the vacancy pair separation, providing further extrapolation test of each model's ability to capture the electrostatic effects that govern defect transport.

infographic.key_insight: Long-range ML interatomic potentials better capture electrostatic defect interactions in SrTiO3 than a short-range baseline, making them more suitable for charged-defect energetics and transport.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Accurate prediction of vacancy formation and migration barriers in perovskites can improve defect engineering, reliability, and ionic transport design for functional oxide materials.
method: Benchmarked MACE-POLAR, MACE-LES, and LOREM against short-range MACE
Started with synthetic point-charge systems, then moved to first-principles SrTiO3 defect data
Evaluated Sr–O Schottky pairs and oxygen-vacancy migration using CI-NEB and molecular dynamics
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports a systematic benchmark spanning idealized electrostatic test cases and realistic DFT data, including vacancy-pair separation-dependent activation barriers.
infographic.watch_item: Long-range models still must disentangle Coulombic effects from DFT screening and other energy contributions, so gains may not transfer uniformly across materials or defect types.
infographic.paper_title: Long-Range Machine Learning Interatomic Potentials for Defect Energetics in SrTiO$_3$

title: Ontology-Grounded, Reasoner-Verified Benchmarks for Evaluating LLM Reasoning in Scientific AI
authors: Nishtha N. Vaidya, Stephan Grimm, Thomas Hubauer, Thomas A. Runkler
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly underpin scientific AI applications that reason over structured knowledge, from biomedical question answering to materials informatics. However, their logical reasoning often falls short, producing factual inaccuracies unacceptable in these settings. Reliable evaluation remains challenging: manual dataset construction scales poorly, and LLM-based generation risks embedding the very flaws it aims to measure. High-quality benchmarks must ground both correct and incorrect labelled examples in explicit background knowledge, formally verifiable by a standard reasoner. We propose a pipeline that automatically generates ontology-grounded multiple-choice question (MCQ) benchmarks from any sufficiently axiomatised OWL 2 ontology, with correct answers grounded in the ontology by design. Distractors are generated by perturbing the right-hand-side class expressions of class definition axioms, and their incorrectness is formally verified by an OWL reasoner via entailment checks. We evaluate the pipeline on three ontologies: Pizza (small, academic), PMDco (complex, materials science), and DOID (large, biomedical), generating 112, 2,491, and 15,216 MCQs respectively. Distractors span four semantic categories from class unsatisfiability to weakened subsumptions, enabling diagnostic evaluation of specific reasoning failures. Items meet natural language quality standards: mean LLM judge scores of 4.02, 4.36, and 3.36 out of 5 confirm fluency, and correct-answer-to-distractor similarity above 0.8 shows that wrong options cannot be dismissed on surface form alone. Six LLMs evaluated zero-shot achieve 41.1-76.8% accuracy, well above the 25% random-guessing baseline, indicating the benchmarks are challenging and discriminative. This work is a step towards more reliable benchmarks for assessing logical reasoning in scientific AI.

infographic.key_insight: The paper introduces a fully automated way to build ontology-grounded multiple-choice benchmarks where correct answers are entailed by design and distractors are reasoner-verified as wrong.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This provides a practical, scalable testbed for measuring and diagnosing logical reasoning in LLMs used for scientific AI, including materials and biomedical knowledge tasks.
method: Generate MCQs from sufficiently axiomatised OWL 2 ontologies.
Create distractors by perturbing the right-hand side of class-definition axioms.
Use OWL reasoner entailment checks to verify distractors are formally incorrect.
infographic.evidence_signal: The pipeline produced 112, 2,491, and 15,216 MCQs on Pizza, PMDco, and DOID, with zero-shot LLM accuracy ranging from 41.1% to 76.8% versus a 25% random baseline.
infographic.watch_item: Benchmark quality depends on the completeness and axiomatization of the source ontology, so sparse or inconsistent ontologies may limit coverage or validity.
infographic.paper_title: Ontology-Grounded, Reasoner-Verified Benchmarks for Evaluating LLM Reasoning in Scientific AI

title: Autocata: Reaction-network-guided autonomous catalyst screening via capability-centric AI
authors: Ruili Li, Rui Qi, Qingqing Mao, Ritankar Das, Beien Zhu, Yi Gao
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) has expanded the accessible space for catalyst discovery, yet executing complex screening campaigns still requires constant human intervention to bridge high-level reaction objectives with underlying computational pipelines. Here, we present Autocata, a knowledge-embedded autonomous agent that scales catalytic expertise by encoding multistep reaction pathways into reusable, language-invocable capabilities. Powered by a Transformer pretrained on two million catalyst-adsorbate structures, the system incorporates a capability registry of 79 adsorbate-specialized generative models spanning complex reaction networks across carbon, nitrogen, oxygen, and hydrogen intermediates. Given a high-level natural-language prompt, Autocata deconstructs reaction networks, queries and configures matching generative models, generates candidate surface configurations, enforces physical and geometric validity filtering, and coordinates machine-learning potentials evaluations to rank promising materials. Crucially, the agent adaptively reconfigures workflows when encountering capability boundaries or task bottlenecks. We demonstrate these capabilities across CH4 activation, nitrogen reduction reaction (N2RR), and CO2-to-methanol pathways. By shifting from static toolkits to an adaptive, language-driven computational infrastructure, Autocata lowers the barrier for expert-level catalyst discovery and offers a scalable paradigm for self-driving catalytic research.

infographic.key_insight: Autocata turns catalyst screening into a language-driven, capability-centric workflow that automatically maps reaction-network goals to specialized generative models and evaluation pipelines.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach could reduce expert bottlenecks in computational catalyst design by automating multi-step setup, candidate generation, validity checks, and ranking across complex reaction pathways.
method: Pretrained a Transformer on 2 million catalyst–adsorbate structures to learn chemistry-aware representations.
Built a registry of 79 adsorbate-specialized generative models covering carbon, nitrogen, oxygen, and hydrogen intermediates.
Uses an autonomous agent to parse natural-language goals, select capabilities, generate candidates, filter invalid structures, and run ML-potential evaluations.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports demonstrations on CH4 activation, nitrogen reduction, and CO2-to-methanol pathways, showing the system can execute and reconfigure screening workflows across multiple reaction networks.
infographic.watch_item: Performance may depend on the coverage and accuracy of the capability registry, so tasks outside the embedded reaction-network models could still require human intervention.
infographic.paper_title: Autocata: Reaction-network-guided autonomous catalyst screening via capability-centric AI

title: AbsorbEvo: An Agentic Framework for Autonomous Inverse Design of Microwave Absorbers
authors: Zhicheng Feng, Yubo Zhao, Xuefeng Yao
abstract: Designing high-performance microwave absorbers requires specialized expertise in electromagnetic theory, materials science and simulation programming, and entails time-consuming optimization. Here, we present AbsorbEvo, an agentic framework for autonomous inverse design that translates natural-language performance objectives into designs verified by full-wave simulations. Its candidate evolution strategy integrates language reasoning, physics-based prediction and historical feedback. A large language model proposes the directions and magnitudes of parameter adjustments based on task objectives and computational history. The system combines directed increments with global sampling to generate candidates and uses a low-cost predictive model as a physics prior to rank them. Only high-ranking designs undergo full-wave simulation. Results passing physical validity checks are used to evaluate performance and guide subsequent search. Experience from training tasks is further distilled into textual skills, which are independently validated before use in new tasks. Under identical proposal budgets on held-out AbsorbBench-36 tasks, AbsorbEvo achieved a task success rate of 79.17%, versus 25.00% for a generic agent and 12.50% for random search. Its mean best coverage was 0.7816, compared with 0.6434 and 0.6448, respectively. By integrating language reasoning and physics-based feedback into design decisions, AbsorbEvo provides a methodological foundation for natural-language-driven autonomous inverse design of microwave absorbers.

infographic.key_insight: AbsorbEvo turns natural-language absorber targets into autonomous candidate design, ranking, and simulation loops that combine LLM reasoning with physics-guided prediction and feedback.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework could substantially reduce expert effort and search time for microwave absorber inverse design while keeping final candidates grounded in full-wave electromagnetic simulation.
method: LLM proposes parameter adjustment directions and magnitudes from the task objective and search history.
A low-cost predictive model acts as a physics prior to rank globally sampled and incrementally evolved candidates.
Top-ranked designs are validated by full-wave simulation, and successful skills are distilled into reusable text instructions.
infographic.evidence_signal: On AbsorbBench-36, AbsorbEvo reached a 79.17% task success rate and 0.7816 mean best coverage, outperforming a generic agent and random search under the same proposal budget.
infographic.watch_item: Performance depends on the quality of the predictive prior, physical validity checks, and task-specific skill transfer, so robustness outside the benchmark and to new absorber families remains to be verified.
infographic.paper_title: AbsorbEvo: An Agentic Framework for Autonomous Inverse Design of Microwave Absorbers

title: Topo-Spectral Percolation Descriptors for Mechanistic Ion Transport Pathways from Static Crystal Structures
authors: Diptendu Roy, Chiku Parida, Juan María García-Lastra, Arghya Bhowmik
abstract: Ion transport controls the macroscopic performance of solid electrolytes, battery electrodes, ion-selective membranes, electrolysis ceramics, mixed conductors, porous sorbents, and biological channels. In each case, ion transport is determined by structural characteristics, namely the available diffusion pathways and the specific bottleneck atoms that limit the ionic jumps. These are intrinsic properties of the crystalline framework, whereas temperature, carrier concentration, and correlated motion govern the transport rate. Ab initio molecular dynamics (AIMD) resolves the mechanism directly but is too costly for materials screening, and most surrogate models give only a single transport number. Here we present a calibration-free method for determining the mechanism, based on Topo-Spectral Percolation Descriptors (TSPD). TSPD obtains the transport mechanism from a single static structure in seconds. It constructs a periodic migration network whose edge barriers are computed from physics-based energetics. We then analyze the barrier-threshold topology of this network and the spectrum of its barrier-weighted graph Laplacian. To establish its validity for computational solid-state ionics, we test TSPD against AIMD ion densities and neutron diffraction data for eight materials, including cathodes and solid electrolytes, whose transport ranges from one- to three-dimensional. TSPD reproduces the established mechanism in every case and correctly identifies structures in which geometric openness does not imply viable ion percolation. The method is most informative for pathway-limited, direction-dependent transport, and it complements full dynamical simulations for strongly cooperative or nearly isotropic transport.

infographic.key_insight: Topo-Spectral Percolation Descriptors (TSPD) can infer ion-transport pathways and dimensionality directly from a single static crystal structure by combining barrier-based migration networks with spectral graph analysis.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This provides a fast, calibration-free screening tool for identifying mechanistic bottlenecks in solid electrolytes, electrodes, membranes, and related ion-conducting materials before expensive dynamical simulations.
method: Build a periodic migration network from the crystal structure and assign physics-based edge barriers.
Analyze barrier-threshold percolation to find accessible diffusion pathways and bottlenecks.
Use the spectrum of the barrier-weighted graph Laplacian to characterize transport dimensionality and mechanism.
infographic.evidence_signal: The method was validated against AIMD ion densities and neutron diffraction for eight materials spanning 1D to 3D transport, and it reproduced the established mechanism in every case.
infographic.watch_item: TSPD is most informative for pathway-limited, direction-dependent transport and may be less definitive for strongly cooperative or nearly isotropic ion motion.
infographic.paper_title: Topo-Spectral Percolation Descriptors for Mechanistic Ion Transport Pathways from Static Crystal Structures

title: MyTm: An Automated Melting Temperature Calculation Toolkit
authors: Y. S. Huang, H. X. Song, Y. Sun, J. L. Li, Y. L. Xu, F. C. Wu
abstract: Melting temperature calculation is one of the important topics in computational materials science. In high-throughput in silico screening and artificial intelligence assisted design of materials, it usually requires a rapid and autonomous assessment of the melting temperature of the target. Unfortunately, molecular dynamics (MD) simulations of the melting point require many cumbersome and manual operations, making large-scale calculation of the melting point challenging. In this work, we introduce MyTm, a toolkit that employs MD to automatically determine the melting point. The method is fully modularized, and by combining these modules, the program enables fully automated melting calculations by using commonly adopted approaches, including the direct-heating method, the void method, the modified void method, the solid-liquid coexistence method, and the Z method. Moreover, a machine learning (ML) method is proposed and employed to recognize and classify the solid like and liquid like atoms, which effectively resolve the low accuracy issue in conventional classification approaches, thus making the automated high throughput pipeline of melting-point calculation possible. The robustness and efficacy of MyTm have been demonstrated by several well studied systems.

infographic.key_insight: MyTm automates melting-temperature prediction with a modular MD toolkit, adding ML-based atom classification to enable high-throughput, hands-off workflows.
infographic.engineering_relevance: It reduces the manual burden of melting-point calculations, making rapid screening and materials design more scalable in computational materials engineering.
method: Implements multiple standard MD melting-point approaches: direct-heating, void, modified void, solid-liquid coexistence, and Z method.
Uses modular program components so users can combine steps into fully automated pipelines.
Adds an ML classifier to distinguish solid-like vs liquid-like atoms more accurately than conventional rules.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract states that robustness and efficacy were demonstrated on several well-studied systems.
infographic.watch_item: Performance likely depends on the quality of the ML classifier and on careful setup of MD protocols for each material system.
infographic.paper_title: MyTm: An Automated Melting Temperature Calculation Toolkit

title: EP-Flow: Disordered Crystal Structure Prediction without Site-Level Annotations
authors: Qiuliang Liu, Liming Wu, Qi Li, Zhonglong Peng, Chang Chen, Xiaolong Chen
abstract: Generative models have made rapid progress in ordered crystal structure prediction, yet many functional materials are intrinsically disordered, with substitutional mixing, vacancies, or interstitial species controlling their properties. Existing crystal generators either assume deterministic site occupations or require site-level disorder annotations, which are often unavailable when the chemical formula is the primary input. We formulate disordered crystal structure prediction through an Occupancy Distribution Matrix (ODM), a continuous site-by-species representation that unifies ordered crystals, solid solutions, vacancy disorder, and interstitial occupancy. A valid ODM must satisfy coupled site-wise occupancy, mass-conservation, and non-negativity constraints, placing each sample on a formula-dependent transportation polytope. We propose Entropic Polytope Flow (EP-Flow), a marginal-constrained flow matching framework that canonicalizes heterogeneous polytopes into a shared double-centered space, learns a marginal-preserving flow, and recovers feasible occupancies through a Sinkhorn inverse map. By jointly generating occupancies, fractional coordinates, and lattice parameters, EP-Flow achieves state-of-the-art performance on formula-conditioned disordered CSP benchmarks derived from COD and MPDS, substantially outperforming adapted ordered-crystal generators. Analyses further show that EP-Flow recovers sparse and chemically meaningful local disorder patterns rather than merely matching global composition statistics.

infographic.key_insight: EP-Flow reframes disordered crystal prediction as generating a physically valid occupancy distribution matrix, enabling disorder modeling without site-level annotations.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This matters for designing functional materials with vacancy, substitutional, or interstitial disorder when only the chemical formula is known.
method: Represents disorder with an Occupancy Distribution Matrix (ODM) that unifies ordered and disordered crystals.
Canonicalizes formula-dependent transportation polytopes into a shared double-centered space for learning.
Uses Entropic Polytope Flow with a Sinkhorn inverse map to recover feasible occupancies while jointly predicting coordinates and lattice parameters.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports state-of-the-art results on formula-conditioned disordered crystal structure prediction benchmarks derived from COD and MPDS, with improved recovery of sparse, chemically meaningful local disorder.
infographic.watch_item: The approach depends on solving constrained transport and Sinkhorn-based inversion, which may add computational overhead and sensitivity to optimization stability.
infographic.paper_title: EP-Flow: Disordered Crystal Structure Prediction without Site-Level Annotations

title: CompMat-Bench: Benchmarking AI Agents for Computational Materials Science
authors: Chenmu Zhang, Levi Felix, Jun-Jie Zhang, Xingfu Li, Xuelian Jiang, Tao Jiang
abstract: Evaluating AI agents on scientific research tasks is constrained by the time and resources required for the underlying experiments or calculations. In computational materials research, repeating the same expensive simulations across agents and trials can make evaluation impractical. We introduce CompMat-Bench, a benchmark of 94 tasks derived from recently published computational materials studies, each asking agents to complete a step toward achieving the study's scientific goal. We reproduce the research steps in advance and assess agents on preparing inputs and analyzing outputs for expensive simulations, so expensive simulations can be avoided during evaluation. The reproduced inputs and results serve as ground truth for grading agents with fixed rules, without an LLM judge. The benchmark supports four evaluation conditions: single tasks and workflows composed of related tasks, each with full or reduced methodological guidance. With full guidance on single tasks, agents based on three LLMs demonstrate the ability to complete individual materials research steps, with pass rates of 66.0-90.4% across 94 tasks. Both longer workflows and reduced guidance can limit agent performance, but in different ways for different agents: they lower the pass rates of the weaker agents, whereas the strongest agent falls only when a long workflow is combined with reduced guidance. Failure analysis attributes most failures to scientific errors rather than to errors in software usage. CompMat-Bench provides a basis for comparing agents on the steps of real materials research and for analyzing agent failure modes.

infographic.key_insight: CompMat-Bench is a 94-task benchmark that evaluates AI agents on real computational materials research steps without rerunning expensive simulations.
infographic.engineering_relevance: It gives materials scientists a practical, reproducible way to compare agents on input preparation, output analysis, and workflow execution under controlled guidance.
method: Derived 94 tasks from recent computational materials papers
Precomputed simulation inputs and outputs as fixed ground truth for rule-based scoring
Tested agents under single-task vs workflow settings, with full vs reduced methodological guidance
infographic.evidence_signal: Across 94 tasks, agents based on three LLMs achieved 66.0-90.4% pass rates on single tasks with full guidance, while longer workflows and reduced guidance lowered performance.
infographic.watch_item: Benchmark results may still depend on how closely task templates and fixed rules match real research workflows, so generalization to open-ended studies should be checked.
infographic.paper_title: CompMat-Bench: Benchmarking AI Agents for Computational Materials Science

title: Linear-Scaling Quantum Transport from Machine-Learning Density Functional Theory Hamiltonians
authors: Bang Liu, Yang Zhong, Zhi-Xin Guo, Xin-Gao Gong, Hongjun Xiang
abstract: Quantum transport simulations that combine density functional theory (DFT) with the nonequilibrium Green's function formalism (DFT-NEGF) are important to modern technology, yet their unfavorable scaling has long confined predictive simulations to small, idealized systems far below the ten-thousand-atom scale of realistic devices. Here, we introduce HamGNN-NEGF, a linear-scaling framework with DFT-level fidelity. An E(3)-equivariant graph neural network trained on conventional DFT Hamiltonians of small structures predicts Hamiltonians for large devices, avoiding costly DFT-NEGF training data. The predicted Hamiltonians are integrated with DFT-derived electrode self-energies, a nonorthogonal kernel polynomial method for Fermi-level determination, and a recursive Green's function algorithm, yielding a computational cost that scales linearly with device length at fixed cross section. Even for devices containing fewer than 500 atoms, HamGNN-NEGF achieves speedups exceeding three orders of magnitude over fully self-consistent DFT-NEGF, with the advantage increasing further with system size. Benchmarks on pristine Pt-Si-Pt, doped Pt-Si:P-Pt, and Pt-molecule-Pt junctions demonstrate meV-level Hamiltonian accuracy, faithful transmission spectra, and predictive simulations beyond 10,000 atoms. Eliminating transport self-consistency also enables hybrid functionals such as HSE06 without additional NEGF overhead, while a zero-bias Hamiltonian approximation extends the framework to finite-bias transport in weakly nonlinear regimes. HamGNN-NEGF thus bridges first-principles accuracy and device-scale simulation, providing a practical route toward predictive modeling of realistic nanoelectronic and quantum devices.

infographic.key_insight: HamGNN-NEGF uses a machine-learned DFT Hamiltonian plus efficient Green’s-function solvers to deliver near-DFT transport accuracy with linear scaling in device length.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This makes predictive quantum transport feasible for realistic nanoelectronic devices with thousands to over 10,000 atoms at dramatically lower cost than self-consistent DFT-NEGF.
method: Train an E(3)-equivariant GNN on conventional DFT Hamiltonians for small structures.
Predict large-device Hamiltonians and combine them with DFT-derived electrode self-energies.
Use nonorthogonal kernel polynomial methods and recursive Green’s functions to compute transport efficiently.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports meV-level Hamiltonian accuracy, faithful transmission spectra, and speedups exceeding three orders of magnitude on Pt-Si-Pt, doped Pt-Si:P-Pt, and Pt-molecule-Pt benchmarks, including systems beyond 10,000 atoms.
infographic.watch_item: The zero-bias Hamiltonian approximation for finite-bias transport is stated to be reliable only in weakly nonlinear regimes.
infographic.paper_title: Linear-Scaling Quantum Transport from Machine-Learning Density Functional Theory Hamiltonians

title: Characterization and Quantification of Immiscible Polymer Blend Compatibilization by Phyllosilicate Clays
authors: Ankit Patidar, Gaurav Goel
abstract: Phyllosilicate clays are widely used in polymer nanocomposites owing to their high anisotropy and tunable surface polarity. Their distribution and interface localization in polymer blends can be used to tune the properties of polymer-clay nanocomposites (PCNCs). A coarse-grained (CG) force field for clays can aid molecular simulations in PCNC development. Here, we developed MARTINI-3 parameters, a CG force field with high chemical specificity, for phyllosilicate clays with diverse surface polarities. Initial interactions for the clay functional groups were determined from hydration free energies, obtained by applying the Lifshitz theory to experimental surface tension data. These were fine-tuned using the structural, thermodynamic, and dynamic properties of thermoplastic starch (TPS)-clay composites from all-atom (AA) molecular dynamics (MD) simulations. The radial distribution function and two-body excess entropy of TPS components, not used in CG parameterization, were accurately estimated, establishing the robustness of the parameters. We investigated the effect of clay surface polarity on polymer segmental dynamics and structure-property relationships. The CG parameters were then used to study the effect of dodecyltrimethylammonium (C12TAB)-modified montmorillonite (MMT), an organically-modified MMT, on TPS-polyethylene (PE) blend morphology using large time- and length-scale MD simulations. We observed compatibilization of the TPS-PE interphase by the amphiphilic clay particle, reducing the TPS-PE interfacial tension from 45 mN/m to 13.06 mN/m. We found good agreement between MARTINI-3 estimates for properties of model MMT-based PCNCs and those from AA simulations and experimental data, establishing grounds for the transferability of the parameters to other systems.

infographic.key_insight: MARTINI-3 coarse-grained clay parameters accurately capture phyllosilicate polarity and show that amphiphilic clay can strongly compatibilize immiscible TPS-PE blends by lowering interfacial tension.
infographic.engineering_relevance: These validated CG clay models enable faster, larger-scale simulation-driven design of polymer-clay nanocomposites with tunable morphology and improved blend compatibility.
method: Derived initial clay-group interactions from hydration free energies using Lifshitz theory and experimental surface tension data.
Fine-tuned parameters against all-atom TPS-clay structure, thermodynamics, and dynamics.
Applied the CG model to C12TAB-modified MMT in TPS-PE blends to predict interphase compatibilization and morphology.
infographic.evidence_signal: The model reproduced structural and dynamic observables from all-atom simulations and estimated TPS component radial distribution and excess entropy accurately, while predicting TPS-PE interfacial tension reduction from 45 mN/m to 13.06 mN/m.
infographic.watch_item: Transferability is promising but still depends on how well the clay surface chemistry, organic modifiers, and polymer chemistry match the calibration/validation cases.
infographic.paper_title: Characterization and Quantification of Immiscible Polymer Blend Compatibilization by Phyllosilicate Clays

title: PPO-HRAP: Proximal Policy Optimization with a Hybrid Regime-Aware Policy for Risk-Controlled Trading
authors: Duong Hien Chi Kien, Thanh Trung Huynh
abstract: Reinforcement learning for trading often struggles to balance upside participation with drawdown control. Profit-only policies can collapse toward passive long exposure on upward-drifting assets, while aggressively risk-penalized rewards can become too defensive during volatile periods. This paper proposes PPO-HRAP, a hybrid regime-aware policy that combines Proximal Policy Optimization with an interpretable regime prior. The agent observes both market features and portfolio-state variables, receives a reward combining portfolio log return, VIX-conditioned drawdown-increase penalty, target-exposure deviation, and turnover cost, and executes a blended action between the PPO actor output and a regime-derived target exposure. On the held-out 2020-2022 SPY test window, PPO-HRAP achieves 27.62% total return, 8.48% annualized return, 0.6447 Sharpe ratio, 0.8588 Sortino ratio, and 0.4592 Calmar ratio, while reducing maximum drawdown from 34.10% for Buy and Hold to 18.47%. Across five SPY seeds, PPO-HRAP remains stable with mean total return $0.2725 \pm 0.0109$ and mean Sharpe ratio $0.6219 \pm 0.0565$. Single-run cross-asset tests on QQQ and DIA further show that the proposed method ranks first on total return and Sharpe ratio for all three reported assets. These results suggest that blending learned actions with a volatility-aware regime prior is a practical way to improve risk-adjusted trading behavior, although the current policy still incurs high turnover and cross-asset robustness beyond SPY remains limited to single-run evidence.

infographic.key_insight: PPO-HRAP improves risk-controlled trading by blending PPO decisions with a volatility-aware regime prior, helping capture upside while limiting drawdown.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach is relevant for deploying reinforcement-learning trading systems that must optimize return and risk simultaneously under changing market regimes.
method: PPO actor learns from market features and portfolio-state variables.
Reward combines log return, VIX-conditioned drawdown penalty, target-exposure deviation, and turnover cost.
Final action is a blend of PPO output and regime-derived target exposure.
infographic.evidence_signal: On SPY test data (2020–2022), PPO-HRAP achieved 27.62% total return and reduced max drawdown to 18.47%, outperforming Buy and Hold on risk-adjusted metrics.
infographic.watch_item: The method still shows high turnover, and cross-asset robustness is supported only by single-run results on QQQ and DIA.
infographic.paper_title: PPO-HRAP: Proximal Policy Optimization with a Hybrid Regime-Aware Policy for Risk-Controlled Trading

title: Measuring trainable degrees of freedom in materials graph neural networks: a random-subspace intrinsic dimension analysis
authors: Shehroz Ahmad Shoaib, Kangming Li
abstract: Final predictive accuracy is the standard basis for comparing graph neural networks (GNNs) in materials-property prediction, but it does not show how strongly performance depends on access to trainable parameter-space directions. Here, we introduce trainable-degree dependence as a complementary characterization of materials GNN learning. Using random-subspace intrinsic-dimension analysis, we train CGCNN, ALIGNN, and DimeNet++ in randomly oriented parameter subspaces across six prediction tasks and measure how performance recovers as independent trainable degrees of freedom are restored. The resulting recovery curves separate endpoint accuracy from the trainable-dimensional demand required to recover it. They reveal distinctions that final errors alone miss: metallic classification and log-bulk-modulus regression recover near-reference performance from small fractional subspaces, formation-energy and band-gap prediction show stronger architecture dependence, and phonon prediction is most sensitive to dimensional restriction. Dataset-size sweeps show that band-gap models require larger fractional subspaces as training data grows, whereas formation-energy and bulk-modulus responses are more stable. A width sweep shows that fractional thresholds can remain stable while absolute threshold dimensions increase with model size. Random-subspace analysis therefore provides a targeted stress test for how materials GNNs use their optimization space.

infographic.key_insight: Materials GNNs can achieve similar final accuracy with very different amounts of trainable parameter-space freedom, and random-subspace recovery curves expose that hidden dependence.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This gives practitioners a model-selection and robustness test beyond accuracy, helping identify architectures that are easier to optimize under constrained capacity or weaker training conditions.
method: Train CGCNN, ALIGNN, and DimeNet++ in randomly oriented parameter subspaces.
Measure how performance recovers as more independent trainable degrees of freedom are restored.
Compare recovery across six materials-property prediction tasks, plus dataset-size and width sweeps.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across six tasks, the recovery curves show that metallic classification and log-bulk-modulus are robust to strong dimensional restriction, while phonon prediction is the most sensitive and band-gap/formation-energy depend more on architecture and dataset size.
infographic.watch_item: Random-subspace results depend on the chosen training setup and subspace sampling, so the fractional-dimension thresholds should be interpreted as comparative diagnostics rather than universal constants.
infographic.paper_title: Measuring trainable degrees of freedom in materials graph neural networks: a random-subspace intrinsic dimension analysis

title: Stress-based structure optimization for a range-separated hybrid van der Waals density functional
authors: Per Hyldgaard, Yunqi Shao, Raul Quintero-Monsebaiz, Lars Öhrström
abstract: Complex matter, often partly soft and pliable, is the generic form of material systems. We must therefore generally call on density functional theory (DFT) to first predict the atomic structure before we can use it to also characterize (expected) properties. A recent range-separated hybrid (RSH) van Waals density functional (vdW-DF), `vdW-DF2-ahbr' (abbreviated AHBR) [PRX 12, 041003 (2022)], shows promise as a high-accuracy predictor of both binding energies and structure, from molecules to solids. However, the present implementation in Quantum Espresso (QE) does not, in our experience, support robust stress-based unit-cell optimization of RSHs. Here we document and illustrate work enabling practical AHBR-based complex-matter discovery: We port the AHBR XC functional to the Vienna Ab Initio Simulation Package (VASP) where use of stress-based DFT optimization is already stable also for RSHs. We test the implementation by comparing high-accuracy AHBR-QE and AHBR-VASP predictions of non-covalent molecular interactions and for structure and cohesion of simple bulk structures. We also illustrate and test the use of the new AHBR-VASP implementation to predict and understand (atomic and anti-ferromagnetic) structure in distorted-rocksalt metal monoxides. Finally, we illustrate use for complex-soft-matter discovery by predicting motifs for layer stacking in the C2N covalent-organic framework (COF) system [Nat. Commun. 6, 6486 (2015)].

infographic.key_insight: The paper makes stress-based unit-cell optimization practical for the AHBR range-separated hybrid vdW functional by porting it from Quantum Espresso to VASP, enabling more robust structure prediction for complex matter.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This improves high-accuracy DFT workflows for materials discovery by combining reliable geometry optimization with a functional that can capture both cohesion and noncovalent interactions.
method: Ported the AHBR exchange-correlation functional from QE to VASP.
Validated the implementation on molecular interactions and simple bulk structure/cohesion benchmarks.
Applied it to difficult structure-prediction cases in distorted-rocksalt metal monoxides and the C2N COF.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports cross-code comparisons between AHBR-QE and AHBR-VASP for noncovalent molecular interactions, bulk structure and cohesion, plus application to magnetic and layered soft-matter systems.
infographic.watch_item: The main concern is implementation-specific robustness: the original QE setup did not support stable stress-based optimization for RSHs, so portability and numerical consistency must be checked carefully.
infographic.paper_title: Stress-based structure optimization for a range-separated hybrid van der Waals density functional

title: Electronic Coupling and Charge-Transfer Landscape of Graphene on Ge(001)/Si(001): Multiscale Analysis Assisted by Machine Learning
authors: Pawel Dabrowski, Przemysław Przybysz, Maciej Rogala, Iaroslav Lutsyk, Paweł Krukowski, Witold Kozłowski
abstract: Understanding and controlling charge transfer at graphene-semiconductor interfaces is essential for the integration of two-dimensional materials into silicon-compatible technologies. Here, we combine ultraviolet photoelectron spectroscopy (UPS), Kelvin probe force microscopy (KPFM), angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (ARPES), scanning tunneling spectroscopy (STS) and density functional theory (DFT) to resolve work-function modulation and electronic coupling in graphene grown on Ge(001)/Si(001). UPS and KPFM reveal a spatially non-uniform work-function landscape correlated with the nanofaceted morphology of the substrate. ARPES and DFT calculations for the pristine interface consistently indicate n-type doping and electron transfer from Ge to graphene. In contrast, modeling of the oxidized interface predicts a reversal to p-type doping, providing a plausible explanation for the different doping polarities reported in the literature. Machine-learning-assisted classification of the STS data resolves distinct local electronic regimes, ranging from nearly free-standing graphene on nanofacet tops to more strongly coupled inter-facet regions and nanoribbon-like regions with distinct local electronic responses. By identifying the mechanisms governing local graphene-substrate interactions and charge transfer, our study provides guidelines for tailoring the synthesis process and minimizing defect formation during delamination. These insights support the production of high-quality graphene layers for electronic devices and for transfer as protective coatings for air-sensitive materials.

infographic.key_insight: Graphene on Ge(001)/Si(001) shows a spatially non-uniform charge-transfer landscape, where pristine regions are n-doped by electron transfer from Ge, but oxidation can flip the interface to p-type behavior.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Understanding and controlling this local electronic coupling helps optimize graphene growth and delamination on Si-compatible substrates for electronic devices and protective transfer layers.
method: UPS + KPFM mapped work-function variation across the surface
ARPES + DFT established the pristine-interface doping trend
STS with machine-learning classification separated distinct local electronic regimes
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports consistent agreement across UPS, KPFM, ARPES, STS, and DFT, with local signals tied to nanofaceted morphology and different interface chemistries.
infographic.watch_item: The doping polarity depends strongly on oxidation and local morphology, so device performance may vary unless the interface state is tightly controlled during synthesis and transfer.
infographic.paper_title: Electronic Coupling and Charge-Transfer Landscape of Graphene on Ge(001)/Si(001): Multiscale Analysis Assisted by Machine Learning

title: Fixed-point neural samplers on discrete spaces
authors: Jiajun He, Denis Blessing, Mouyang Cheng, Yuanqi Du, Carles Domingo-Enrich
abstract: Sampling from discrete, unnormalized distributions without access to data is a challenging problem. Neural samplers offer a promising approach by training generative models from density evaluations directly. Despite recent progress, existing discrete neural samplers are prone to mode collapse, come without convergence guarantees when trained via fixed-point iterations, and are often tied to a specific reference process such as masked or uniform diffusion. In this work, we introduce Discrete Gibbs Iterative Neural Sampler, a fixed-point neural sampler that addresses these limitations, enabling efficient, scalable learning, substantially reducing mode collapse in practice. Our framework builds on masked diffusion and also extends to transport between pairs of distributions. We demonstrate that the resulting method scales effectively to high-dimensional systems, supports amortized sampling across different conditions, and enables accurate estimation of alloy phase diagrams.

infographic.key_insight: Discrete Gibbs Iterative Neural Sampler is a fixed-point neural sampler for discrete, unnormalized distributions that improves robustness against mode collapse while keeping sampling efficient and scalable.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The method can support practical materials discovery workflows by enabling amortized sampling across conditions and accurate estimation of alloy phase diagrams from density evaluations alone.
method: Builds a fixed-point neural sampling framework on masked diffusion for discrete spaces.
Uses iterative Gibbs-style updates to learn from density evaluations without data samples.
Extends the framework to transport between pairs of distributions for conditional or cross-distribution sampling.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports that the method scales to high-dimensional systems, substantially reduces mode collapse in practice, and enables accurate alloy phase diagram estimation.
infographic.watch_item: Because the approach relies on fixed-point iterations, convergence behavior and sensitivity to the chosen reference process or update schedule should be validated carefully in new implementations.
infographic.paper_title: Fixed-point neural samplers on discrete spaces

title: Learning ab initio phase-field models
authors: Mengyi Chen, Peichen Zhong, Zihan Zhang, Qianxiao Li
abstract: Simulating microstructure evolution requires quantum-mechanical accuracy and mesoscopic reach in length and time scales, a combination that no current method achieves. Classical phase-field models provide this reach, but their accuracy is limited by phenomenological free energies and mobilities. Here we develop a framework for learning ab initio phase-field models, where the mesoscopic equation is not postulated but derived from a Mori-Zwanzig projection of molecular dynamics onto species-density fields under explicit assumptions. The nonlocal free energy and mobility left unspecified by this equation are parametrized by neural networks and learned from short molecular dynamics trajectories generated with machine-learning interatomic potentials of ab initio accuracy. We demonstrate the framework on an iron-boron melt and on hydrogen-helium mixtures under planetary conditions. For iron-boron, the model shows that the melt at the FeB$_4$ composition is spinodally unstable at ambient pressure but stabilized at 10 GPa, offering a thermodynamic rationale for why FeB$_4$ has been synthesized only under high pressure. For hydrogen-helium, the model predicts the immiscibility boundary and captures droplet nucleation and growth in helium-rain simulations of a column corresponding to 2.2 million atoms, far beyond the scale of atomistic modeling at comparable accuracy. Trained across compositions and conditions, such models could provide a mesoscopic counterpart to ab initio molecular dynamics.

infographic.key_insight: The paper learns phase-field models directly from ab initio-quality molecular dynamics by deriving the mesoscopic equation from Mori-Zwanzig projection and fitting the unknown free energy and mobility with neural networks.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This enables quantum-accurate microstructure evolution simulations at mesoscopic length and time scales, making it useful for predicting phase stability, segregation, and nucleation in materials under realistic conditions.
method: Derive a phase-field equation from molecular dynamics using Mori-Zwanzig projection onto species-density fields.
Parameterize the unknown nonlocal free energy and mobility with neural networks.
Train on short MD trajectories generated by machine-learning interatomic potentials of ab initio accuracy.
infographic.evidence_signal: The approach is validated on Fe-B and H-He systems, reproducing the FeB4 pressure-dependent stability shift and the helium-rain immiscibility/nucleation behavior in a 2.2-million-atom equivalent column simulation.
infographic.watch_item: Model reliability depends on the quality and coverage of the training trajectories, so extrapolation to unseen compositions or conditions may be uncertain.
infographic.paper_title: Learning ab initio phase-field models
